2. Facts leading, to filing of this civil appeal, in short, are that the petitioner as plaintiff filed Title Suit No.109 of 2002 before the Court of Assistant Judge, Damurhuda, Chuadanga for mandatory injunction to compel the defendant-Respondent Nos.1-11, to appoint the plaintiff-petitioner as Religious Teacher in Natuda Secondary High School who secured first position in the appointment test amongst the female candidates as per the Employment Notice published in the "Daily Jugantar" dated 2-6-2002 by removing the defendant-Respondent No.11-Md Abu Sadek Sadek Ali Khondokar, to the effect that 30% quota is to be filled up with female teacher as per the direction of the Government vide Memo No.১১/বিবিধ-৩১/১৬(অংশ-১)/(৩৪৯৬৫০) তারিখ ১৩-১-১৯৯৯. That the School authorities-respondents published Advertisement in "The Daily Jugantar" on 2-6-2002 for appointment of a teacher for Natuda High School in the Subject of Religion and she applied for the said post. There was a circular of the Government, through the Ministry of Education vide Memo No.11/Misc-31/16(part-1)/34 (650) dated 13-1-1999. That 30% of the teacher of the school should be filled up by female candidates. As there was no female teacher in the said school and as the plaintiff stood first amongst the female candidates in the examination, she should be given preference in getting that job. In spite of that, the school authority did not take any step to appoint her as teacher of the said school. On 22-6-2002, the plaintiff filed an application to the defendant No.1 for getting her appointment for the said post but the defendant No.1 did not appoint her. Thereafter, the plaintiff instituted the instant suit for mandatory injunction with a prayer for direction upon the defendant No.1 to appoint her as teacher of the said school and allow her to join in the post. By way of amendment of the plaint the plaintiff stated that she came to know that on 29-6-2002, the school authority appointed the defendant No.11 as teacher of the said subject which was illegal and, as such, she filed the instant suit for mandatory injunction with a prayer for the aforesaid relief. Hence, the suit. 

 11. Mr Md Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellant has submitted that the High Court Division has no power to interfered in the finding of facts of the learned trial Court as well as the Court of appeal below as the last Court of finding of facts concurrently found from the record and evidence that the defendants violated the law and decision of the Government in not appointing the appellant in the post of the 'Religion Teacher' and by appointing the defendant No.11 in that post by ousting the appellant who is in a good position in the merit list and stood first amongst the female candidates and, as such, the appeal may be allowed by setting aside the judgment of the High Court Division. He has further submitted that the High Court Division committed an error of law in not holding that the circular being Memo No.11/Misc-31/16(part-1)/34(650) dated 13-1-1999 contained direction of the Government to appointment 30% of the teachers in all education institutions under the administrative control of the Ministry of Education is of a general application to the appointment of teachers in all educational Institutions, the circular has the precision of a Rule and has been issued by the Government itself and is in consonance with the prevision of article 28(4) of the Constitution and hence, though it is an administrative instruction, it is an effective and binding as statutory Rules in view of the principle of law laid down in the case reported in 50 DLR (AD) 27 (para-41) and, thereafter, the judgment of the High Court Division reversing the concurrent decision of the Courts below is not sustainable in law. He has next submitted that, the High Court Division fell in an error of law in holding that the defendants have no legal obligation to appoint the appellant as a teacher of the school and the appellant had not acquired any enforceable right to get such direction. In view of the principle of law, laid down in the case reported in 50 DLR (AD) 27 (para-41), the direction of the Government has given in the Circular dated 13-1-1999 to appoint 30% female teachers in all educational institutes in Bangladesh has the force of law imposing legal obligation on the defendants to appoint such female teachers, and the plaintiff who stood first amongst female candidates, has enforceable right to get benefit of such direction and, therefore, the judgment of the High Court Division reversing the concurrent decisions of the Courts below is not sustainable in law. He has finally submitted that the High Court Division fell in an error of law in not considering that, the direction contained in the circular dated 13-1-1999 followed by the resolution dated 29-4-2002 adopted by the Managing Committee of the School to appoint 30% female teachers in the school impose an obligation, on the defendants to appoint 30°k female teachers in the school, and the defendants having acted in breach of their obligation, it is necessary to compel the defendants to comply with the direction issued by the Government and hence, the Court has discretion. under section 55 of the Specific Relief Act to grant injunction to comply performance of the requisite acts by the defendants and, thereafter, the judgment of the High Court Division reversing the concurrent decisions of the Courts below is not sustainable in law. Mr Bhuiyan in support of his contentions relied upon the citations to the case of Principal Secretary, President's Secretariat, Dhaka and others reported in 42 DLR (AD) 214, to the case of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Establishment vs Shafiuddin Ahmed and others reported in 50 DLR (AD) 27 and in the case of Mohan Singh and others vs International Airport Authority of India reported to 9 SCC (1997) 132. Hence, the instant appeal may kindly be allowed. 

 14. Thereafter, he pointed out that the circulars dated 6-8-1998 and 13-1-1999 were not published in the official gazette. So, the argument advanced by the Senior Counsel for the respondent No.10 do not bear any merit. According to decision referred by the learned Counsel for the respondent No.10, 50 DLR (AD) 27 para-41, unless any circular published by the concerned authority in official gazette, the same has no bear status of law, therefore, it is not binding upon the present respondent nor to comply with the direction of the circular is mandatory to the respondents. He referring the same judgment has further argued that it has been decided by the Apex Court, even, any Cabinet's decision without publishing the official gazette cannot be treated as a guideline. Therefore, the decision referred by the learned Counsel for the appellant has no binding effect in the present case. Mr All has further argued that the advertisement for the post of religion teacher was published not specifically for women teachers. But from the language of the advertisement, it appears that the authority concerned published the advertisement for the post of religious teacher in a combined form. Therefore, appointment of the respondent was correct as per merit, because, it is admitted facts that he secured the 1st position in the examination. 

 15. In that view of the matter, the suit for mandatory injunction was not maintainable, because, legal status or right was not infringed to any of the candidate including the plaintiff appellant. Therefore, both the Courts below committed serious error in not considering such legal aspects of the instant case in issuing mandatory injunction. 

 The High Court Division committed an error of law in not holding that the Circular notified in Memo No. 11/Misc-31/16-(Part-1)/34(650); dated 13-1-1999 containing direction of the Government to appoint 30% of the teachers in all educational institutions under the administrative control of the Ministry of Education is of general application to the appointment of teachers in all educational institutions, the circular has the precision of a Rule and has bean passed by the Government itself and is in consonance with the provision of Article 28(4) of the Constitution and hence, though it is an administrative instruction, it is as effective and binding as statutory Rules in view of the principle of law laid down in the case reported in 50 DLR (AD) 27 (Para-41) and, therefore, the judgment of the High Court Division reversing the concurrent decisions of the Courts below, is not sustainable in law. The High Court Division fell in an error of law in holding that the defendants have no legal obligation to appoint the plaintiff as a teacher of the school and the plaintiff had not acquire any enforceable right to get such direction. In view of the principle of law laid down in the reported in 50 DLR (AD) 27 (Para-41) the direction of the Government notified in the circular dated 13-1-1999 to appoint 30% female teachers in all educational institutions in Bangladesh has the force of law imposing legal obligation on the defendants to appoint such female teachers, and the plaintiff, who stood first among female candidates, has enforceable right to get such direction and, therefore, the judgment of the High Court Division reversing the concurrent decisions of the Courts below is not sustainable in law. The High Court Division fell in an error of law in not considering that the direction contained in the circular dated 13-1-1999 followed by the resolution dated 29-4-2002 adopted by the Managing Committee of the School to appoint 30% female teachers in the school imposes an obligation on the defendants to appoint 30% female teachers in the school, and the defendants having acted in breach of their obligation, it is necessary to compel the defendants to comply with the direction issued by the Government and hence the Court has discretion under section 53 of the Specific Relief Act to grant injunction to compel performance of the requisite acts by the defendants and, therefore, the judgments of the High Court Division reversing the concurrent decision of the Courts below is not sustainable. 

 20. A scrupulous appraisal of the section demonstrates that a Court of law can provide mandatory injunction if it is required to compel the performance of certain acts which the Court is capable of enforcing and also to compel performance of the requisite acts to prevent the breach of an obligation by the defendant(s) and to get a relief in a suit as in the instant case, the plaintiff must satisfy the Court by producing evidence that the defendants had an obligation to her which they were breaching. 

 21. In this very case the Trial as well as the lower Appellate Court arrived on concurrent findings that the school authority had a legal obligation as such was bound to appoint the present appellant in the post of teacher of religion. 

 22. It is the long standing established cardinal principle of appreciation of evidence that finding of facts, whether concurrent or not, arrived at by the trial and lower appellate court is impervious from intrusion in revisional jurisdiction, apart from in certain well definite circumstances such as non-consideration and misreading of material evidence affecting the merit of the case, or misconception, misapplication or misapprehension of law. It has been settled in the legendary case of Srimati Bibhabati Devi vs Ramendra Narayan Roy and others (AIR 1947 PC 19) (Popularly known as Bhawal Raja's case} citing cases of Umrao Begum vs Irshad Husain (1894) LR 21 IA 163; Kunwar Sanwal Singh vs Rani Satrupa Kunwar (1905) LR 33 IA 53, 54 and Rani Srimati vs Khajendra Narayan Singh (1904) LR 31 IA 127, 131 Privy Council the then highest Court of appeal opined that if the appellants failed to show any miscarriage of justice, or the violation of any principle of law or procedure, therefore, see no reason for departing from the usual practice of this Board of declining to interfere with two concurrent findings on pure questions of fact. As the successor of the highest Court this Division still maintains this principle in both civil as well as criminal jurisdiction. The same was dictated in the case of Shamser AU (Md) and others vs Mosammat Kafizan Bibi, reported in 44 DLR (AD) 231 and reiterated in the case of Md Habibur Rahman Bhuiyan and others vs Mosammat Galman Begum and others reported in 2013 BLD (AD) 93 = 64 DLR (AD) 133. 

 25. This misconception, misapplication or misapprehension of legal scheme of the matter in question is the very reason that played pivotal role in decreeing the suit in favour of the instant appellant by the Courts below, as we understood; which clearly affects the merit of the case and made miscarriage of justice, as well as it is the violation of principle of law. As such, we opine that High Court Division has rightly interfered in the decisions of the Courts below. 

 26. Further, our considered view is that the citations referred by the learned Senior Counsel for the appellant are not helpful for the instant appeal, because, the facts and circumstances of the case in hand and the referred cases are quite distinguishable. 

 27. Regarding the nature of the relief of mandatory injunction, in the case of Md Abdul Karim and others vs Syed Enayet Karim and others reported in LEX/BDAD/0067/2021 this Division observed that: 

 "Having considered the entire material on record, we hold the view that the plaintiffs sought for an order of mandatory injunction along with some allied relief. But granting an order of mandatory injunction is rarest of the rare case and the plaintiff is to come with clear breast with a view to seek such equitable and specific relief. ... Over and above, this type of injunction cannot be granted specially where there is apprehension to suffer internal and external management and smooth function of an educational institution." 

 28. From the discussions above we observe that this is not a fit case for granting an order of mandatory injunction; rather, if mandatory injunction is granted there is apprehension to suffer internal and external management and smooth function of an educational institution. 

 29. As such, this Division find no non-consideration or misreading of the material evidence on record or an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice or such finding is found to have resulted from glaring misconception of law or misconception, misapplication or misapprehension of law in the judgment and order of the High Court Division.
